title: Growth Laws for Wrinkly Surfaces
text:
The difference between a perfectly flat leaf and a wavy, wrinkly one comes down to a battle between differntial growth and elastic energy minimisation. The shapes of leaves are governed by the laws of non-Euclidean elasticity and differential geometry.
To understand why a leaf wrinkles, we can look at Gaussian curvature (K), which is the product of the two principal curvature of a surface.

title: Logarithmic Spiral
text: Logarithmic spirals in plants are a striking example of geometry in nature, where botanical structures grow according to the Golden Ratio and the Fibonacci sequence.

title: Logarithmic Spiral
text:
Spiralling Succulents
Many varieties of succulents arrange their leaves outward from a central point along an expanding logarithmic trajectry to ensure uniform access to sunlight and water collection.

title: Logarithmic Spiral
text:
Sunflower Seed Heads
The packing of seeds in a sunflower head features two sets of overlapping logarithmic spirals - one running clockwise and the other anticlockwise - maximising the number of seeds that can fit into the centre.

title: Logarithmic Spiral
text:
Pinecone Scale Arrangements
Pinecones exhibit steep logarithmic spirals formed by their scaling bracts, tightly safeguarding the seeds inside.

title: Fractal
text:
A fractal is a structure that possessed the property of . Specifically, it refers to a structure where the exact same shape repeatedly appears when the entire figure is broken down into several smaller parts.



Fractal pattern in fern leave


While fractal patterns and shapes appear complex at first glance, they are actually the result of repeating simple rules and operations.
While fractals are a concept rooted in geometry, the fractal approach can also be applied to analyse various phenomena, such as stock prices, currency fluctuations, and social structures.
Many examples of fractals can also be observed in the natural world. These include a wide variety of examples, such as , (like turbn shells and nautiluses), the shapes of cumulonimbus clouds, and the circulatory system in the human body (including the heart, blood vessels, and lymphatic vessels).

title: The Analemma Project
text:
Artist Lucy Smith created the Analemma Project sculpture. She completed her PhD “Making the Conceptual Tangible: The Role of Art in Communicating Science” here at the University of Dundee.
The Analemma is an unequal figure-of-eight shape, created by tracking the sun’s position in the sky at the same time each day over a period of one year.

title: Phyllotaxis
text:
Plants arrange their leaves around a stem in regular patterns. The angle between one leaf and the next is called the divergence angle, and this pattern of leaf arrangement is known as phyllotaxis. Many different plant species share similar phyllotaxis patterns, and these can be described using a small number of mathematical patterns.
Which of the following leaf arrangement pattern do you find in this plant? Please record the number of each leaf arrangement pattern in the table provided on the Maths Trail map.

title: Phyllotaxis
text:
Distichous (\(180^\circ\))
Leaves grow on alternating sides of the stem, forming a flat, two-sided pattern.

title: Phyllotaxis
text:
Fibonacci Spiral (\(137.5^\circ\))
Leaves grow around the stem in a tight spiral, using the golden angle to make the best use of space and get as much light as possible.

title: Phyllotaxis
text:
Decussate (\(90^\circ\))
Leaves grow in pairs, with each pair turned at a right angle to the pair below.

title: Phyllotaxis
text:
Tricussate (\(60^\circ\))
Three leaves grow from the same point on the stem, spaced evenly around it. Each group of three is rotated \(60^\circ\) around the stem from the group below.

title: Helicopter Seeds
text:
The seeds from maple, elm and ash trees have curved wings to let them stay in the air longer. The wind will pick up these seeds and carry them to suitable groud. These seeds twirl and spin around. They will then drop and sprount a new tree. Some people call these seeds because they look like and can spin like a propeller.
Here you will learn how to make your own spinner.

Fold the middle flap in the opposite direction of the other two flaps. Put the paper clip on the end of the middle flap.
Find a maple seed spinner. Drop both spinners from the same height and compare how they spind. Does your spinner work as well as nature’s?
